name: Garland Green
lede: Garland Green is a muted yellowish green that Maerz and Paul recorded in their 1930 color dictionary, and no other system in our library has repeated the name since.

sections.title: A 1930 dictionary entry
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* places Garland Green on plate 22, swatch H7, first recorded in 1928 [1]. A color this close would be filed by the ISCC-NBS system as a moderate yellowish green, with a Munsell notation of 6.4GY 5.1/4.7 [1]. No other system in our library repeats the name, so it carries no plate numbers beyond Maerz and Paul's own [1].

It sits in our library's Greens family alongside [[khaki-green]] and [[moss-green]], and the closest common color word is [[moss|Moss]], about nine units away in CIEDE2000 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Garland Green covers at least five percent of the canvas in 226 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.95 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens narrows that to 96 [2]. That puts it ahead of 58 percent of the named colors we track by presence [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 26 of 1,674 paintings, at 1.6 percent of that decade's paintings, 3.4 times the archive's overall rate, and it plays an accent, rather than a shadow or mid-tone, in 40 percent of its 96 appearances [2].

Georges Seurat is its most devoted painter here, using it in nine of his 41 paintings in the archive, 12.1 times the rate of the museums those works come from [2]. It is also most over-represented in French paintings, at 2.3 times the expected rate [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1390, nearly 540 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that the color existed as a material that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
